clinical_knowledge.topic: Hereditary Angioedema (C1-inhibitor deficiency) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hereditary Angioedema (C1-inhibitor deficiency) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management is bradykinin-targeted (e.g., C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant, or ecallantide) rather than antihistamines, epinephrine, or corticosteroids, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent sudden episodes of severe lip swelling and abdominal cramps without itchy hives

Key HPI features: 32F with family history presenting with non-pruritic, non-urticarial lip/hand swelling and colicky abdominal pain. Low C4 and C1 esterase inhibitor levels; unresponsive to antihistamines/epinephrine.
Objective/Exam findings: Non-pitting, non-pruritic edema of the lips and hand without urticarial wheals; low C4 with low C1 esterase inhibitor antigenic and functional levels.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hereditary Angioedema (C1-inhibitor deficiency).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Allergic angioedema without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Laryngeal swelling with voice change or stridor.
management_principles: Treat attacks early — especially any laryngeal involvement — with an on-demand bradykinin-targeted therapy (IV C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant, or ecallantide) rather than antihistamines or epinephrine
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Hereditary Angioedema C1 Inhibitor Deficiency: recurrent sudden episodes of severe lip swelling and abdominal cramps without itchy hives. 32F with family history presenting with non-pruritic, non-urticarial lip/hand swelling and colicky abdominal pain. Low C4 and C1 esterase inhibitor levels; unresponsive to antihistamines/epinephrine.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal between attacks. Non-pitting, non-pruritic edema of the lips and hand without urticarial wheals. Complement C4 low; C1 esterase inhibitor quantitative antigen and functional activity both low.
reference_soap.assessment: Hereditary Angioedema (HAE) Type 1 secondary to C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Treat attacks early with an on-demand bradykinin-targeted therapy (IV C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant, or ecallantide); treat any laryngeal involvement as an airway emergency and prepare for emergency airway management if respiratory compromise progresses. 2. Antihistamines, epinephrine, and corticosteroids do not target bradykinin-mediated HAE and should not delay HAE-specific therapy. 3. Refer to an allergy/immunology specialist for confirmatory testing, individualized long-term prophylaxis, and an emergency action plan.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Hereditary Angioedema C1 Inhibitor Deficiency

teaching.one_liner: Recurrent bradykinin-mediated swelling from low or dysfunctional C1-esterase inhibitor — supported by low C4 plus abnormal C1-INH antigenic and functional testing, not by allergy testing.
red_flags: Laryngeal swelling with voice change or stridor
Severe abdominal attack mimicking an acute abdomen

must_ask.say: Is the swelling itchy, or does it come without any itching or hives?
Does anything seem to set off an episode — stress, minor injury, dental work?
Do you ever get severe abdominal pain with the swelling?
Does this run in your family?
Have antihistamines or epinephrine ever helped?
